newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tokyo plunges as other Asian markets jump.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo plunges as other Asian markets jump.

text.p: Japanese stocks lost over 600 points on Monday after a policy speech by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto failed to soothe nervous investors, while markets in Australia, New Zealand and Taiwan hit fresh highs.

The key Nikkei stock index closed just over 600 points down, but off its lows, reflecting disappointment with a speech to parliament in which Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto vowed to press ahead with tax rises and repeated pledges of broad reforms.

The market's key barometer, the Nikkei 225 average, closed down 609.70 points, or 3.37 percent, at 17,480.34. It had briefly dived around 850 points to 17,237.27 ahead of the speech as the market guessed accurately that Hashimoto would have little new to say to bolster confidence in the stock market.
The Nikkei plunged over 2,000 points in the first trading week of 1997 on worries that the government's forthcoming tax increases could derail Japan's fragile economic recovery.
Elsewhere in Asia, markets were bouyant after Wall Street's 68-point or one percent leap on Friday to a new record high.
In Australia, strength on Wall Street, combined with hopes of a further local interest rate cut, boosted the Australian share market to a record close.
The benchmark All Ordinaries index finished 8.7 points firmer at 2,444.2, eclipsing its previous record close of 2,348.2 which was set on January 15.

New Zealand's top 40 share index ended within striking distance of a three-year high. The NZSE-40 Capital Index ended 10.65 points stronger at 2,440.21, its highest level since reaching 2,444.80 in early February, 1994.
"The market seemed to lose a bit of its early enthusiasm after lunch. I think a bit of caution crept in when the Nikkei strated to slide again," a Sydney-based broker said.
South Korean stocks closed sharply higher on hopes of a political solution to labour unrest after President Kim Young-sam's proposal to discuss the crisis with opposition leaders on Tuesday.

"Stock prices rose steadily even when strikes were rampant last week. Kim's offer to have talks with opposition leaders gave the market a big boost," said Kim Choon-kwon, a broker at Daewoo Securities.
The composite stock index closed up 24.23 points or 3.49 percent at 718.46. Brokers said rising fund inflows and falling interest rates also boosted buying sentiment.
In Taiwan, share prices surged 1.40 percent to notch their highest close since June 1990 on hopes of a renewed rally around the February 7 Chinese lunar new year, brokers said.
The weighted TAIEX index gained 100.12 points to 7,254.32, surpassing the 7,206.42 point close of January 16, which until Monday was the highest level since 7,339.71 on June 5, 1990.
But in Hong Kong, stocks were flat in afternoon trade, paring the morning's gains as the market consolidated its recent move to record ground.
The Hang Seng Index was up 11.84 points, or 0.09 percent, at 13,868.24 after rallying to a session high of 13,994.86 during the morning.

"I think a pause for breath is probably a bit overdue. It's doing quite well to hold onto its gains," said Archie Hart, director at BZW Asia. He expected the Hang Seng to make a run for 14,000 points later this week.
